Note · Heath & Heath — Switch

4 min read851 wordsUpdated 2026-06-06notes/canon/canon-heath-switch.md

Canon · Cluster: Culture & Change · Maps to E5 (Transformation & Change Management)

  • Source: Chip & Dan Heath, Switch: How to Change Things When Change Is Hard (2010)
  • Core claim: Change is a conflict between the rational mind (Rider) and the emotional mind (Elephant), traveling a Path (the environment). Most change efforts fail because they coach the Rider and ignore the Elephant.
  • Framework — Direct / Motivate / Shape:
  • Direct the Rider — give crystal-clear direction (what looks like resistance is often confusion). Find the bright spots (what's already working) and clone them; script the critical moves.
  • Motivate the Elephant — make people feel something (analysis doesn't move people, emotion does); shrink the change so it feels doable; grow a "growth mindset" identity.
  • Shape the Path — make the right behavior easier: tweak the environment, build habits, rally the herd. Change the situation, not the person.
  • Applies when: you need behavior change in individuals or small groups and willpower-based approaches have failed — especially when "resistance" might actually be ambiguity or a hostile environment.
  • Breaks when: it's strongest on individual/team behavior, weaker on the political and structural obstacles of large transformations where Kotter's coalition-building is needed (canon kotter leading change). "Make it easy / shape the path" can mask that the underlying system (Meadows) or culture assumptions (Schein) are the real blockers, not the path. And "bright spots" assumes a working example exists — sometimes nothing yet works.

  • Practitioner counterpoint: (researched 2026-06-05 — r/managers corpus + Kotter/Schein transcripts) The corpus confirms Switch's central diagnosis — "resistance" is usually unclear direction (Rider) or a hostile Path, not bad will. In r/managers' "How Do You Talk to an Employee Who Isn't Getting Promoted…" (4,470↑, 2,187 comments) a manager's own first instinct is to Shape the Path — "Change the policy / have core hours… I would love that" — but, blocked, defaults to coaching the Rider alone, which "just keeps him apace." The book's blind spot also shows: the most-upvoted change story, "The 'silent resignation' nobody notices" (9,404↑, 1,026 comments), is a demotivated Elephant — "they still deliver, still smile in meetings but the spark's gone" after "too many ignored ideas" — and the thread's verdict is brutally un-Heath: "once they hit that point, it's rare to get them back." Shrinking-the-change and bright-spots don't reload a burned-out Elephant. The Rider/Elephant is Kahneman's System 2/1 in change clothing (canon kahneman thinking fast and slow).

  • Researched layer (2026-06-05)

  • Canonical explanation (sourced): Switch's core move is to stop coaching only the rational Rider and make people feel the change — the same lever Kotter's own team names: "This is about what is it going to feel like and what is it going to look like when we're successful… how do we ensure people can see themselves in that success" (Kotter International). The EPM summary frames it identically — "you want to win the hearts and minds… create a willing army of people who want to make the change happen" — i.e. Motivate the Elephant before you Direct the Rider.
  • The Path, verified: the corpus echoes Switch's "change the situation, not the person" — Schein's model literally makes "create the right environment" a discrete change step (EPM, Schein explainer), and stresses "culture ultimately comes about through the behavior of individuals" — behavior first, beliefs follow, exactly Heath's Path → habit logic.
  • Real application (mined): the Craig case (r/managers, 4,470↑) is a clean three-lever miss — the Path is locked (flex-time policy the manager "can't change"), the Elephant isn't engaged (Craig is "frustrated… passed over so many times"), and the Rider was never given a clear, scripted next move ("should I have a frank discussion why other people tend to grow faster?"). Switch's prescription — script the critical move + remove one friction point — is precisely what's absent.
  • Where the corpus pushes back on the book: practitioners report a failure mode Switch under-weights — the Elephant that's already quit. In "the silent resignation" (9,404↑), the spark dies from structural causes (ignored ideas, endless urgent work) and is "rare to get back"; bright-spots and shrink-the-change assume a willing animal. And Kotter's emphasis on a guiding coalition + sense of urgency is the political/structural layer Heath admits Switch is weak on (canon kotter leading change).
  • Sources in corpus: Kotter International Inc — "Kotter's 8 Steps for Leading Change" (youtube.com/watch?v=SGYmPMcgDPg) · EPM — "Kotter's 8-Step Change Model Explained" (22coAwMD9M0) · EPM — "Edgar Schein's Culture Model Explained with Example" (HM89E6ltVOg) · r/managers "How Do You Talk to an Employee Who Isn't Getting Promoted…" (4,470↑), "The 'silent resignation' nobody notices" (9,404↑).
  • Links: canon kotter leading change · canon kahneman thinking fast and slow · canon clear atomic habits · canon schein organizational culture

Rep

For a change that's stuck, do all three: script one clear next move (Rider), find a feeling or bright spot (Elephant), and remove one point of friction (Path). Notice which was actually missing.

Marks itself read when you reach the end.
